note.overview: Firms can reduce the risk of rare disasters by accounting for more frequent near misses: precursor events that could have escalated to a disaster but did not. Investigating a near miss reveals its root cause, allowing the firm to improve process safety and reduce disaster risk. A managing firm, however, usually does not directly observe the occurrence of a near miss but instead relies on the report of an agent (an employee or contractor) who is also responsible for precautionary measures that prevent such incidents.

models.summary: Firms can reduce the risk of rare disasters by accounting for more frequent near misses: precursor events that could have escalated to a disaster but did not. Investigating a near miss reveals its root cause, allowing the firm to improve process safety and reduce disaster risk. This paper explains why near-miss reporting may not take place in such a decentralized setting.

source.quote: Investigating a near miss reveals its root cause, allowing the firm to improve process safety and reduce disaster risk.

A managing firm, however, usually does not directly observe the occurrence of a near miss but instead relies on the report of an agent (an employee or contractor) who is also responsible for precautionary measures that prevent such incidents.

Methodology: We examine the firm’s problem through a dynamic principal-agent model that captures the agent’s potential for under-reporting near misses along with moral hazard related to their precautionary effort.
The reason is that disasters are a signal of the agent’s unveriﬁable precautionary effort.
The contract with the agent speciﬁes payments wH,t,wD,t contingent on the current-period outcome (high output or disaster).

conditions: Instead, the principal focuses on existing precautionary measures at the expense of reporting, even though reporting would seemingly lead to a “win-win” outcome.

Recall that the agent may lose from improvement (ΔπA 2 < 0) because it substitutes for precautionary effort, but could conversely gain from improvement (ΔπA 2 > 0) as it reduces the likelihood of disasters.
In particular, whenever the agent’s gain ΔπA 2 ≠0, the agent’s tradeoff is misaligned with that of the principal in that the agent’s tradeoff also influences the equilibrium effort.
Equally, the principal may not elicit reports even when both parties stand to gain from safety improvement: ΔπP 2,ΔπA 2 > 0.

conditions: We have seen that the principal may fail to capitalize on near-miss reports when the subsequent process improvements may hurt the agent, that is, ΔπA 2 < 0.
Indeed, as we have seen, simply allowing wR > 0 does not suffice to prevent under-reporting.
In the first period, the principal may now set a payment wRH ≥0, which the agent receives if they report a near miss that leads to improvement and subsequent safe operation in the second period.

Specifically, the principal may set a reporting bonus in the first period, which the agent receives in the second period—but only following subsequent continued safe operation after safety improvement.
